transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-17 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48 min | Attendees: Jordan, Priya (Redwood); Carlos, Sara, Tom (NimbusPay)

Summary: quick run through of long-context + high TPS edge behavior. Demo included simulated payment chat logs concatenated to 80k tokens, 500 TPS burst for 2 minutes, and intentional websocket stalls to trigger backpressure and timeout logic.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE, and with me is Priya our solutions engineer. How's NimbusPay doing today?
[00:07] Carlos: Good, thanks. Busy quarter. We wanna make sure our fraud chat flows survive stupid large histories — we keep full transaction trails and that hits the context limit. So, can you show what happens if we feed an 80k token history and then slam with traffic?
[00:22] Priya: Yep, that's exactly what we prepared. We'll do three things: long-context run, TPS surge, and simulate intermittent client stalls to exercise streaming backpressure and timeouts.
[00:34] Sara: Quick security note before you spin up anything — Tom needs to know where logs and payloads go. We have strict PII removal rules.
[00:40] Tom: Right, SOC2 box ticked, but we need KMS control and audit logs.
[00:45] Jordan: Totally, we'll cover the control plane visibility and KMS. Priya, can you start the long-context demo?
[00:50] Priya: Sure. Loading a synthetic concat of user transactions and support chat — we pushed it to the model as a single session with 80k tokens. Running on a dedicated instance with prefix KV cache warmed. Note: some ASR mis-transcriptions on the call — the demo console logs say 80,312 tokens.
[01:10] Priya: (share screen) You can see the request hits the routing layer, chooses a big-window variant (we use an extended context profile), and the runtime splits into chunked attention passes. The runtime uses chunked KV flushing and a sliding truncation window to preserve recent 8k tokens while material older history is offloaded to prefix cache entries.
[01:35] Carlos: When that offload happens, is there a risk of semantic loss? For example, if a user references a prior payment note from 50k tokens ago.
[01:45] Priya: Yes, there's a tradeoff. We keep a prioritized summary cache for older history — minibatched summarization — but it's lossy. For strict determinism we recommend app-level stitching: store canonical metadata in your DB and include exact references in the prompt.
[02:05] Sara: So if we need 100% fidelity for audit scenarios, we should avoid blind truncation?
[02:12] Priya: Correct. For audit-grade transcripts you can route those requests to Redwood Dedicated pinned with a policy to keep full KV cache in memory; that costs more but preserves fidelity.
[02:25] Jordan: Okay next, TPS surge. We're going to pump 500 TPS for two minutes against the same endpoint to show autoscaling and graceful fallback.
[02:34] Priya: Kicking it off now. You might see increased queue times and then fallback to a lighter quantized model if capacity saturates.
[02:44] (audible churn in logs)
[02:48] Priya: Alright, at ~30s we see the first backpressure event. The router trimmed batch windows and applied request shedding for the lowest priority routes — note the per-token cost dropped but latency increased slightly for some sessions.
[03:05] Carlos: When shedding happens how do you notify the client? We want to avoid silent failures.
[03:11] Priya: We return an explicit 429 with a structured body when we drop requests, and for streaming we emit a terminal frame indicating graceful fallback with a reason code. The client SDK also supports configurable retries with incremental backoff.
[03:26] Tom: If a streaming connection stalls mid-token, do you ever return partial tokens or corrupt frames?
[03:33] Priya: Good point. We flush completed token chunks periodically. If a connection dies mid-chunk we still commit the generated tokens to the session log and the client can reconnect and request resume from last confirmed token index. There are edge cases where the client sees duplicated tokens on resume — we provide idempotency and sequence numbers to reconcile.
[03:55] Sara: We saw in another vendor that reconnects caused repeated assistant replies; is your sequence numbering reliable across region failovers?
[04:04] Priya: Yes, sequence numbers are assigned at the write-ahead layer and survive region handoff. But if the session is sharded across multiple GPUs with different KV caches, you can hit inconsistency. Our recommended pattern is single-shard session pinning for critical flows.
[04:22] Jordan: I'm going to switch the test to create artificial websocket stalls — drop the TCP for a few seconds to force backpressure lanes.
[04:30] (timeout simulation begins)
[04:40] Priya: Okay at 5s of stall the client connection enters stalled state. The runtime will keep generating into a short-term buffer up to a TTL (we use 30s by default) and then either flush to storage or abort if storage quotas are exceeded.
[04:58] Carlos: That TTL seems short for mobile clients. Can it be tuned?
[05:02] Priya: Yes, TTL and buffer sizes are per-route configs; we can increase to 2 minutes for your mobile use, though that increases memory footprint. For very long stalls we recommend using resumable uploads and checkpointing tokens to durable store.
[05:20] Tom: And those buffers are encrypted at rest?
[05:23] Priya: Yes, everything persisted uses customer-managed KMS if configured for Private or Dedicated; hosted default uses Redwood-managed KMS but we can do customer-managed under enterprise contract.
[05:34] Sara: Any logs that might contain PII we need to mask upstream — does Redwood provide hooks?
[05:39] Jordan: We do. There's a pre-ingest redact hook and an eval pipeline to run scrubbers. We'll send the redact policy and sample config.
[05:50] Priya: Back to the demo: the stall ended, connection resumed, and the client asked for resume from token index 12,345. The runtime replayed tokens 12,346 onwards. You can see we deduped a pair of tokens that overlapped.
[06:10] Carlos: What about long-running sessions — like multi-hour chats with continuous append — how do you prevent the KV cache from growing unbounded?
[06:19] Priya: We have eviction strategies: LRU-based TTL, summarization tiers, and manual snapshot/flush API. For sessions that must be infinite, we recommend periodic compaction: generate a summary checkpoint every N messages and store the rest off-node.
[06:36] Jordan: Now we'll show a forced timeout case: we set request timeout to 8s on client and purposefully push a heavy attention block to exceed that to show partial response behavior.
[06:47] Priya: Kicking heavy prompt now. At 8s the client times out and closes. The server detected a timeout and emitted a partial response frame with code PARTIAL_GEN; you can see the structured body with last_token_index and resume_token.
[07:10] Sara: If we resume, does the model re-simulate missing context and produce non-deterministic output?
[07:16] Priya: There is nondeterminism across resumed runs, yes. We support deterministic sampling (fixed seed/temperature zero) for audit scenarios but that impacts quality. For user-facing chat we allow some randomness but provide attribution to indicate a resumed partial.
[07:32] Carlos: Ok, switching gears — can you run a short failure recovery where the primary region goes down and requests failover to another region with a different model variant?
[07:42] Priya: Yes — initiating region failover. Note: failing over will pick a compatible model variant; we'll hit an embedding/schema mismatch for some custom tokenizers and we surfaced best-effort transliteration.
[07:58] (logs)
[08:05] Priya: Failover completed. A few sessions got a note that the model variant changed; we applied cookie-based session affinity for pinned sessions to avoid variant jumbling.
[08:20] Tom: For compliance we need an audit trail of any model variant changes per session.
[08:25] Jordan: The console emits a model-change event with timestamp and reason; we'll send examples.
[08:33] Priya: We're 10 minutes in; switching to console to show telemetry. (shares console) Here's per-route token latency distribution, queue depth, and the backpressure events annotated. You can filter to the time window of the surge.
[08:51] Carlos: Nice, seeing the queue percentile spikes. Are the heuristics that trigger shedding tunable?
[08:56] Priya: Yes — you control the priority tiers, per-route SLAs, and the router's masking for low-priority traffic. We also have an Optimize suggestion engine that will propose batch sizes and KV profiles to reduce cost.
[09:10] Sara: How much does Dedicated buy us for these edge cases? Is it purely capacity or are there behavioral differences?
[09:17] Priya: Dedicated gives pinned GPUs, single-tenant caches, and you can disable shedding for pinned sessions at the cost of available throughput — basically stronger fidelity guarantees.
[09:30] Carlos: Any RTO/RPO guarantees?
[09:33] Jordan: Our Dedicated SLA includes an uptime SLA and an operational RTO for failovers; we'll share the SLA doc.
[09:40] Priya: One more subtlety: when you run high TPS with long context, memory pressure can cause background KV eviction which increases tail-latency spikes. We instrument that and surface a 'history eviction' metric so you can correlate regressions.
[09:58] Carlos: If we see tail latency spikes, do you offer automatic model fallback to a smaller context model to reduce mem pressure?
[10:05] Priya: Yes, routing rules can fallback to a quantized smaller-window model. The tradeoff is loss of older context. You can also configure a hybrid: route non-critical traffic to small-window and pin critical sessions.
[10:18] (client Q&A)
[10:25] Tom: For KMS integrations — HSM support?
[10:28] Jordan: We integrate with most cloud KMS and can support bring-your-own-HSM for Private deployments.
[10:34] Sara: Can we get logs of the actual token indexes and sequence numbers for a session? We need to match to internal transaction ids.
[10:42] Priya: Yep, session logs contain token_index, sequence_number, and optional user metadata. Those are available in the audit export.
[10:52] Carlos: We're concerned about cost during the pilot — 500 TPS for two minutes is fine, but what if production has multiple bursts daily?
[11:00] Jordan: Our recommendation: hybrid pattern — reserved capacity for baseline, on-demand burst credits, and Optimize rules to adapt batch sizes based on real-time telemetry to reduce unit cost. We'll model your traffic in the pricing worksheet.
[11:12] Priya: Wrapping up the demo results: long-context run showed summarized fallback for >64k windows, TPS surge triggered shedding under priority policy, websocket stalls used TTL buffer with resumable tokens, and region failover swapped model variants with event audit.
[11:30] Jordan: Quick recap of agreed next steps — we'll provision a 48-hour dedicated pilot, get sample traffic from NimbusPay, and send security artifacts. We'll also run the throughput harness with your prompts.
[11:44] Carlos: Sounds good. One more thing: can you include a short playbook for client-side reconnect logic and idempotency keys?
[11:51] Priya: Absolutely. We'll include SDK patterns and pseudocode.
[11:56] Tom: Thanks, this was helpful — we'll review and Sara will share a compliance checklist.
[12:02] Jordan: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the pilot onboarding doc and a calendar invite for the throughput run.

End of transcript.
